claims.statement: The same TI note gives the eye a Gen 3, 4 and 5 receiver must see after equalisation as an extrapolated eye height of 25, 15 and 15 mV and a minimum eye width of 0.3 UI (37.5, 18.75 and 9.375 ps), and a target bit error rate of 1e-12.
claims.source: PCI Express Base Specification receiver eye requirements, as tabulated by Texas Instruments SNLA426, Table 2-2 and section 4
claims.conditions: Measured after equalisation; TI's own figure is taken before the 3-tap DFE at a redriver output; the specification itself has not been read
claims.note: Table 2-2: 'Extrapolated Eye Height after EQ 25 mV 15 ± 1.5mV 15 ± 1.5mV'; 'Minimum Eye Width after EQ 0.3UI (37.5ps) 0.3UI (18.75 ± 0.55ps) 0.3UI (9.375 ± 0.5ps)'; section 4: 'the targeted BER (1E-12)'; section 3: 'measured post-equalization before the 3-tap DFE blocks. This means at the output of the PCIe redriver'. Source check by Claude Opus 5.5 against the document on 15 Oct 2026; Geetansh asked for this page's upgrade the same day.
claims.source_title: Texas Instruments (V. Flores Prado) — High-Speed PCB Layout for PCIe Gen 5, SNLA426, Jun 2023

claims.statement: The eleven PCIe transmitter presets for 8 GT/s and 16 GT/s are, as preshoot and de-emphasis in dB: P0 0 and -6.0; P1 0 and -3.5; P2 0 and -4.4; P3 0 and -2.5; P4 0 and 0; P5 1.9 and 0; P6 2.5 and 0; P7 3.5 and -6.0; P8 3.5 and -3.5; P9 3.5 and 0; P10 0 and a de-emphasis set by the advertised LF level. De-emphasis = 20 log10(Vb/Va), preshoot = 20 log10(Vc/Vb), boost = 20 log10(Vd/Vb).
claims.source: PCI Express Base Specification transmitter presets, as reproduced by Tektronix, Top 10 Things to Know about PCIe, section 05
claims.conditions: Nominal values; tolerances of ±1 to ±1.5 dB apply; the table is given for Gen 3 and Gen 4
claims.note: Table 'Compliance Presets': 'P4 0 0', 'P1 0 -3.5 ± 1 dB', 'P0 0 -6.0 ± 1.5 dB', 'P9 3.5 ± 1 dB 0', 'P8 3.5 ± 1 dB -3.5 ± 1 dB', 'P7 3.5 ± 1 dB -6.0 ± 1.5 dB', 'P5 1.9 ± 1 dB 0', 'P6 2.5 ± 1 dB 0', 'P3 0 -2.5 ± 1 dB', 'P2 0 -4.4 ± 1.5 dB', 'P10 0 Variable'; 'De-emphasis = 20log10 Vb/Va', 'Preshoot = 20log10 Vc/Vb', 'Boost = 20log10 Vd/Vb'; 'P10 levels are not fixed; its de-emphasis level is a function of the LF level that the Tx advertises during training.' The page's tap coefficients are derived from these dB values, not quoted. Replaces preset values the page carried until 15 Oct 2026 that disagreed with this table (P0 flat, P4 -2.2 dB). Source check by Claude Opus 5.5 against the document on 15 Oct 2026; Geetansh asked for this page's upgrade the same day.
claims.source_title: Tektronix — Top 10 Things to Know about PCIe

claims.statement: PCIe 4.0 kept 128b/130b coding at 16 GT/s; its channel is limited, so longer channels or a second connector need a repeater (redriver or retimer); its receiver test channel is about 12 in with 28 dB of loss; its connector stayed backwards compatible with Gen 1 to 3; it added lane margining, which measures eye height and width margin at the end of the channel; and it lowered the minimum eye height to 15 mVpp.
claims.source: PCI Express Base Specification 4.0, as summarised by Tektronix, Top 10 Things to Know about PCIe, section 02
claims.conditions: As summarised by a test-equipment vendor in 2017
claims.note: '16 GT/s, using scrambling, same as 8 GT/s, no encoding change from Gen3 (128b/130b)'; 'Gen4 connector backwards-compatible with Gen1/2/3'; 'Limited channel: requires use of repeater (both redriver & retimer) for longer channels and/or 2nd connector'; 'Test channel is around 12” long and has a total of -28 dB loss'; 'New Rx Lane Margining feature measures Eye Height (EH)/Eye Width (EW) margin at the end of the channel'; 'The minimum eye height for Gen4 has been reduced to 15mVpp'. Source check by Claude Opus 5.5 against the document on 15 Oct 2026; Geetansh asked for this page's upgrade the same day.
claims.source_title: Tektronix — Top 10 Things to Know about PCIe

claims.statement: PCIe 4.0 and 5.0 transmitters use a 3-tap FFE (one pre-cursor, one post-cursor tap); the PCIe 4.0 reference receiver has a CTLE with 7 configurations and a 2-tap DFE limited to ±30 mV and ±20 mV; the PCIe 5.0 reference receiver has a CTLE with 11 configurations and a 3-tap DFE limited to ±80, ±20 and ±20 mV.
claims.source: PCIe 4 and PCIe 5 Base Specifications, as implemented in MathWorks SerDes Toolbox examples (PCIe4 and PCIe5 Transmitter/Receiver IBIS-AMI Model)
claims.conditions: Reference (behavioural) receivers for compliance, as modelled by a tool vendor
claims.note: PCIe4 page: 'A PCIe4 compliant transmitter uses a 3-tap feed forward equalizer (FFE) with one pre-tap and one post-tap'; 'The Rx CTLE block is set up for 7 configurations'; 'set up for two DFE taps'; '+/-30 mV for tap1 and +/-20 mV for tap2'. PCIe5 page: 'one pre-tap, one main tap, and one post-tap'; '11 configurations (0 through 10)' that 'matches the Poles and Zeros given in the PCIe Gen5 Base Specification'; 'set up for three DFE taps'; tap limits ±80, ±20 and ±20 mV. Consistent with C-129's 3-tap DFE for PCIe 5.0. Source check by Claude Opus 5.5 against the document on 15 Oct 2026; Geetansh asked for this page's upgrade the same day.
claims.source_title: MathWorks — PCIe5 Transmitter/Receiver IBIS-AMI Model (SerDes Toolbox example; PCIe4 example alongside)

claims.statement: PCIe link equalisation runs in four phases inside Recovery.Equalization: in Phase 0 the system sends the add-in card a starting transmitter preset with the speed-change request, at the lower rate; in Phase 1 the two ends reach the new rate with an error ratio no worse than 1e-4 and advertise their equalisation capabilities; in Phase 2 the add-in card adjusts the system's transmitter while tuning its own receiver; in Phase 3 the system adjusts the card's transmitter while tuning its own receiver; on exit the link should run at a bit error ratio of 1e-12 or better.
claims.source: PCI Express Base Specification, Recovery.Equalization, as described by Teledyne LeCroy (Nov 2014)
claims.conditions: Described for 8 GT/s; C-140 gives the same phases at 16 and 32 GT/s
claims.note: 'Phase 0 starts at a rate of 2.5 GT/s. The system (upstream) sends a speed-change request along with a TxEQ preset to the add-in card (downstream)'; 'establish communication with a bit-error rate of at least 10-4'; 'In Phase 1, the system and add-in card advertise their equalization capabilities'; 'In Phase 2, the downstream add-in card adjusts the upstream system's TxEQ settings while tweaking its own RxEQ settings. In Phase 3, that process reverses'; 'operating at a BER of at least 10-12'. Replaces a phase description the page carried until 15 Oct 2026 that had the roles reversed. Source check by Claude Opus 5.5 against the document on 15 Oct 2026; Geetansh asked for this page's upgrade the same day.
claims.source_title: Teledyne LeCroy — An Under-the-Hood View of PCIe 3.0 Link Equalization, Nov 2014

claims.statement: A link trains to 2.5 GT/s and then equalises at 8, 16 and 32 GT/s in turn, with the same four phases at each rate; vendors put each speed step at about 100 ms, about 300 ms to reach 32 GT/s; PCIe 5.0 added two optional modes to shorten this, equalisation bypass to the highest rate and a no-equalisation-required mode.
claims.source: PCI Express Base Specification 5.0, link equalisation, as described by Synopsys (Oct 2019)
claims.conditions: Timing as reported by vendors; the bypass modes are optional
claims.note: 'The link must initially train to L0 at 2.5 GT/s followed by equalization at 8.0 GT/s, 16 GT/s and 32 GT/s sequentially'; 'single speed transition with equalization takes about ~100ms'; 'it would take ~300ms to bring-up link to 32GT/s'; 'The equalization phases (phase 0,1,2,3) for PCIe 5.0 remain the same as the previous generations'; 'Equalization bypass to highest rate' and 'No equalization required' mode. Source check by Claude Opus 5.5 against the document on 15 Oct 2026; Geetansh asked for this page's upgrade the same day.
claims.source_title: Synopsys — Reduce Link Bring-Up Time with PCIe 5.0 Modes, Oct 2019

claims.statement: TI's PCIe Gen 5 layout note gives the loss of 1 in of trace at 8 and 16 GHz as 0.189 and 0.336 dB on Megtron 6, 0.251 and 0.411 dB on Rogers, 0.548 and 1.017 dB on GETEK, 0.578 and 1.078 dB on Nelco 4000-6, 0.686 and 1.289 dB on FR4, and 0.961 and 1.844 dB on tetra-functional FR4.
claims.source: Texas Instruments SNLA426, Table 9-1
claims.conditions: Computed by TI from a closed-form loss formula for one trace geometry; trace only, no vias, connectors or packages
claims.note: Table 9-1 '1" Trace Loss Over Frequency for Various PCB Materials': 'Megtron 6 3.4 0.002 0.189 0.336', 'Roger 3.48 0.0037 0.251 0.411', 'GETEK 4.1 0.011 0.548 1.017', 'Nelco 4000-6 4.0 0.012 0.578 1.078', 'FR4 4.4 0.014 0.686 1.289', 'Tetra Functional FR4 4.1 0.022 0.961 1.844'. Source check by Claude Opus 5.5 against the document on 15 Oct 2026, added after Sonnet's page review.
claims.source_title: Texas Instruments (V. Flores Prado) — High-Speed PCB Layout for PCIe Gen 5, SNLA426, Jun 2023

claims.statement: The PCIe specification allows 70 to 100 ohm differential impedance for high-speed lanes; add-in cards are required to be 85 ohm differential so they interoperate with any root complex and endpoint; the 100 MHz reference clock targets 100 ohm.
claims.source: PCI Express Base and CEM Specifications, impedance, as summarised by Texas Instruments SNLA426 section 10
claims.conditions: As summarised by TI; vias, capacitor pads, connectors and cables are exempt
claims.note: 'The PCIe specification requires 70 to 100 Ω differential impedance. To interoperate with different root complexes and end points, Add-In-Cards require 85 Ω differential impedance. This requirement does not apply to vias, AC coupling capacitor pads, connectors, or cables'; 'the differential 100 MHz reference clock target impedance is 100 Ω'. Source check by Claude Opus 5.5 against the document on 15 Oct 2026, added after Sonnet's page review.
claims.source_title: Texas Instruments (V. Flores Prado) — High-Speed PCB Layout for PCIe Gen 5, SNLA426, Jun 2023

claims.statement: USB 3.0 was first released on 12 November 2008, USB 3.1 on 26 July 2013 and USB 3.2 on 22 September 2017; USB 3.2 Revision 1.1 (June 2022) incorporates errata and ECNs.
claims.source: USB 3.2 Rev 1.1, revision history
claims.conditions: Specification release dates, not product availability
claims.note: Revision history table on the title pages.
claims.source_title: USB-IF — Universal Serial Bus 3.2 Specification, Revision 1.1 (June 2022)

claims.statement: The USB 3.2 specification absorbed all prior USB 3.x specifications and identifies three transfer rates, 20, 10 and 5 Gbps; 20 Gbps is two lanes of 10 Gbps.
claims.source: USB-IF, usb.org/usb-32-0
claims.conditions: Public statement by the standards body
claims.note: 'The USB 3.2 specification absorbed all prior 3.x specifications. USB 3.2 identifies three transfer rates – 20Gbps, 10Gbps, and 5Gbps.'
claims.source_title: USB-IF — USB 3.2 specification page

claims.statement: Gen 1x1 (5 Gbps, 8b/10b) has a raw throughput of 500 MB/s, reduced to 450 MB/s or less at the application; Gen 2x1 (10 Gbps, 128b/132b) about 1.2 GB/s raw and about 1.1 GB/s or less at the application. Both double in x2 operation.
claims.source: USB 3.2 Rev 1.1, section 4.4.11 (Efficiency)
claims.conditions: Best case; hub arbitration and concurrent flows can reduce it further
claims.note: Section 4.4.11 attributes the reduction to flow control, packet framing and protocol overheads.
claims.source_title: USB-IF — Universal Serial Bus 3.2 Specification, Revision 1.1 (June 2022)

claims.statement: Dual-lane operation (Gen 1x2 and Gen 2x2) is supported for USB Type-C only. The Configuration Lane is Lane 0 as set by CC pin decoding, and up to 6400 ps of lane-to-lane skew is allowed at the receiver. A failing link falls back in the order Gen 2x2, Gen 2x1, Gen 1x2, Gen 1x1.
claims.source: USB 3.2 Rev 1.1, section 3.2.1.3 (Dual-Lane Operation) and Table 7-15 (Gen 2x2 PHY capability fallback order)
claims.conditions: USB 3.2 dual-lane operation
claims.note: Table 7-15 notes that a fall from Gen 2x1 to Gen 1x2 addresses failures that 'may be due to link not meeting Gen 2 loss budget'.
claims.source_title: USB-IF — Universal Serial Bus 3.2 Specification, Revision 1.1 (June 2022)

claims.statement: USB 3.2 transmitters swing 0.8 to 1.2 V differential peak-to-peak (nominal 1 V), with a DC differential impedance of 72 to 120 ohms. Gen 1 de-emphasis is 3.0 to 4.0 dB (nominal 3.5 dB). Gen 2 uses a 3-tap FIR equaliser with preshoot 1.2 to 3.2 dB and de-emphasis 2.1 to 7.0 dB, where preshoot = 20 log(Vc/Vb), de-emphasis = 20 log(Vb/Va) and the taps sum to 1.
claims.source: USB 3.2 Rev 1.1, Table 6-18 (Transmitter normative electrical parameters), section 6.7.5 and Table 6-21
claims.conditions: Measured at TP2 or at the compliance breakout board output
claims.note: Revision 1.1 incorporates the TxEQ Equalization Settings ECN, which replaced a nominal setting (preshoot 2.2 +/- 1.0 dB, de-emphasis -3.1 +/- 1.0 dB, informative c-1 = -0.083, c+1 = -0.125, nominal boost 4.7 dB) with the range now in Table 6-21.
claims.source_title: USB-IF — Universal Serial Bus 3.2 Specification, Revision 1.1 (June 2022)

claims.statement: All USB 3.2 transmitters are AC coupled, with 75 to 265 nF coupling capacitors associated with the transmitter, either in the media or in the transmitting component.
claims.source: USB 3.2 Rev 1.1, section 6.2.2 and Table 6-18 (CAC-COUPLING)
claims.conditions: Gen 1 and Gen 2
claims.note: 'The PHYs are required to be AC coupled. The AC coupling capacitors are associated with the transmitter.'
claims.source_title: USB-IF — Universal Serial Bus 3.2 Specification, Revision 1.1 (June 2022)

claims.statement: The transmitter eye is measured at TP4, at the end of the reference channel and a compliant cable, after the reference receiver equaliser: at least 100 mV eye height with at most 0.66 UI total jitter at Gen 1, and at least 70 mV with at most 0.671 UI at Gen 2, measured over 10^6 UI and extrapolated to a 10^-12 bit error ratio.
claims.source: USB 3.2 Rev 1.1, section 6.7.3 and Table 6-20 (Normative transmitter eye mask at TP4)
claims.conditions: Compliance measurement through the reference channels
claims.note: Section 6.7.4: 'At this point the eye may be closed. To open the eye so it can be measured a reference Rx equalizer, is applied to the signal.'
claims.source_title: USB-IF — Universal Serial Bus 3.2 Specification, Revision 1.1 (June 2022)

claims.statement: The reference receiver is a CTLE at Gen 1 and, at Gen 2, a first-order CTLE followed by a one-tap DFE whose coefficient is limited to 0 to 50 mV. For long cables and channels the eye at the receiver is closed until equalisation is applied; the real receiver's equaliser and training are implementation-specific. Receiver equalisation trains on a TSEQ pattern, repeated 65,536 times at Gen 1 and lasting about 8 ms at Gen 2.
claims.source: USB 3.2 Rev 1.1, sections 6.8.2, 6.8.2.1 and 6.8.2.2; section 6.8.1 (Receiver equalization training)
claims.conditions: Informative reference equalisers used for compliance
claims.note: Section 6.8.2: 'For long cables and channels the eye at the Rx is closed, and there is no meaningful eye without first applying an equalization function.'
claims.source_title: USB-IF — Universal Serial Bus 3.2 Specification, Revision 1.1 (June 2022)

claims.statement: The receiver tolerance test sends a compliance pattern with added jitter through the compliance reference channel and checks it in loopback, with SSC present throughout. The sinusoidal-jitter corner is 4.9 MHz at Gen 1 and 7.5 MHz at Gen 2, above which the receiver must tolerate 0.2 and 0.17 UI peak-to-peak. The Gen 2 stimulus uses 2.2 dB preshoot and -3.1 dB de-emphasis.
claims.source: USB 3.2 Rev 1.1, section 6.8.5 and Table 6-28 (Input jitter requirements for Rx tolerance testing)
claims.conditions: Compliance test conditions
claims.note: Table 6-28 note 3: 'During the Rx tolerance test, SSC is generated by test equipment and present at all times.'
claims.source_title: USB-IF — Universal Serial Bus 3.2 Specification, Revision 1.1 (June 2022)

claims.statement: For USB 3.2 Gen 2 a host or device transmitter must drive a total loss of 23 dB at 5 GHz to the far side, while a transmitter in a cable plug next to the receiving port drives 8.5 dB at 5 GHz to the controller receiver.
claims.source: USB Type-C Release 2.5, section 6.1.2.4.6 (USB 3.2 Signal Swing)
claims.conditions: USB 3.2 Gen 2 at its 5 GHz Nyquist frequency
claims.note: Quoted in the active-cable section. The page's split of 8.5 dB to each end and 6 dB to the cable is arithmetic from this row and the cable limit in C-153 (8.5 + 6 + 8.5 = 23), not a table in the specification.
claims.source_title: USB-IF — USB Type-C Cable and Connector Specification, Release 2.5 (March 2026)

claims.statement: Practical Type-C to Type-C cable lengths are up to 2 m for USB 3.2 Gen 1 and up to 1 m for Gen 2 (informative). Normatively, a Gen 2 cable's fitted insertion loss must be no worse than -4 dB at 2.5 GHz, -6 dB at 5 GHz and -11 dB at 10 GHz, and a Gen 1 cable's no worse than -7 dB at 2.5 GHz. Differential-to-common-mode conversion (SCD12/SCD21) must be at most -20 dB for Gen 2 cables and -17 dB for Gen 1 cables, from 100 MHz to 10 GHz.
claims.source: USB Type-C Release 2.5, Table 3-1 and sections 3.7.2.3.1, 3.7.2.3.6, 3.7.2.4.1 and 3.7.2.4.6
claims.conditions: Passive Type-C to Type-C cable assemblies, mated with the test fixture
claims.note: Table 3-1 note: the lengths 'are informative and represent the practical lengths based on cable performance requirements'.
claims.source_title: USB-IF — USB Type-C Cable and Connector Specification, Release 2.5 (March 2026)

claims.statement: Type-C cable and connector S-parameters are normalised to 85 ohms differential, and a mated connector should be within 85 +/- 9 ohms (informative). The raw-cable examples cover both twisted-pair and coaxial construction, with intra-pair skew recommended below 10 ps/m.
claims.source: USB Type-C Release 2.5, section 3.7 preamble, sections 3.7.1.1 and 3.7.1.2 (Tables 3-21 and 3-22), section 3.7.3.1
claims.conditions: Cable and connector; the host or device board impedance is not set here
claims.note: Informative raw-cable and connector targets.
claims.source_title: USB-IF — Universal Serial Bus 3.2 Specification, Revision 1.1 (June 2022)

claims.statement: A Type-C plug fits either way up. The CC pins detect the orientation, which sets the lane ordering of the TX/RX pairs and identifies the Configuration Lane, so that a host or device can route the signals if needed.
claims.source: USB Type-C Release 2.5, sections 2.3.2 and 4.5 (connection flow)
claims.conditions: USB 3.2 over Type-C
claims.note: 'This allows for signal routing, if needed, within a host or device to be established for a successful connection.'
claims.source_title: USB-IF — USB Type-C Cable and Connector Specification, Release 2.5 (March 2026)

claims.statement: USB 3.2 lets a silicon vendor design the channel and the component as a matched pair: compliance is measured through reference channels representing long and short channels, and a silicon component is expected to come with layout guidelines that must be followed for the system to meet the specification.
claims.source: USB 3.2 Rev 1.1, section 6.2.1 (Measurement Overview)
claims.conditions: Gen 1 and Gen 2 compliance methodology
claims.note: 'This methodology allows a silicon vendor to design the channel and the component as a matched pair. It is expected that a silicon component will have layout guidelines that must be followed in order for the component to meet the overall specification and the eye diagram at the end of the compliance channel.'
claims.source_title: USB-IF — Universal Serial Bus 3.2 Specification, Revision 1.1 (June 2022)

claims.statement: JEDEC published UFS 3.0 (JESD220D) on 30 January 2018, the first UFS to use M-PHY HS-Gear4, at up to 11.6 Gbps per lane. It uses M-PHY v4.1 and UniPro v1.8, with two lanes for a maximum of 23.2 Gbps, and uses M-PHY v4.1's Adapt support to monitor and train the channel. It specifies a 2.5 V VCC supply.
claims.source: JEDEC press release, 30 January 2018
claims.conditions: Interface rate is raw, before line coding
claims.note: 'the first standard to introduce MIPI M-PHY HS-Gear4, with a data rate of up to 11.6 Gbps per lane'; 'Continues support of 2-Lanes, max data rate of 23.2 Gbps'; 'Utilizes Adapt support in MIPI M-PHY v4.1 ... by monitoring and training the communication channel'. Read on jedec.org on 18 Oct 2026.
claims.source_title: JEDEC — UFS 3.0 (JESD220D) announcement

claims.statement: JEDEC published UFS 3.1 (JESD220E) on 30 January 2020, still on M-PHY v4.1 and UniPro v1.8. It added DeepSleep, a low-power device state for lower-cost systems whose UFS voltage regulators are shared with other functions.
claims.source: JEDEC press release, 30 January 2020
claims.conditions: Feature list of the release
claims.note: 'references the MIPI M-PHY v4.1 physical layer specification and the MIPI UniPro v1.8 transport layer specification'. Read on jedec.org on 18 Oct 2026.
claims.source_title: JEDEC — UFS 3.1 (JESD220E) announcement

claims.statement: UFS 4.0 (JESD220F, 17 August 2022) uses M-PHY v5.0 and UniPro v2.0 to double the interface bandwidth to about 4.2 GB/s for reads and writes. It also adds High Speed Link Startup and M-PHY's Eye Monitor, lowers VCC from 3.3 V to 2.5 V, and stays backward compatible with UFS 3.1 and 3.0.
claims.source: JEDEC press release, 17 August 2022
claims.conditions: Feature list of the release
claims.note: 'Improved system latencies by enabling High Speed Link Startup'; 'introducing Enhanced Device Error History ... and M-PHY's Eye Monitor'; 'Utilizes a more efficient VCC=2.5V as opposed to the 3.3V supported in the prior version'. Read on jedec.org on 18 Oct 2026.
claims.source_title: JEDEC — JESD220F UFS 4.0 announcement

claims.statement: UFS 4.1 (JESD220G) was announced on 8 January 2025, and JEDEC lists it as superseding UFS 4.0 in December 2024. It keeps M-PHY v5.0 and UniPro v2.0 and about 4.2 GB/s, and is hardware compatible with UFS 4.0; its changes are in the device and host-controller features.
claims.source: JEDEC press release, 8 January 2025; JEDEC JESD220F document page (status line)
claims.conditions: The PHY layer is unchanged from UFS 4.0
claims.note: 'maintaining hardware compatibility to UFS 4.0'; listed changes are host-initiated defragmentation, WriteBooster resize, bootable LUs, RPMB authentication, exception types and QLC preparation. The supersession date is from JEDEC's JESD220F page.
claims.source_title: JEDEC — UFS 4.1 (JESD220G) announcement

claims.statement: UFS 5.0 (JESD220H, 26 February 2026) reaches 46.6 Gb/s per lane per direction with M-PHY HS-G6, and up to about 10.8 GB/s over two lanes. It integrates link equalization, adds a distinct power-supply rail that isolates the PHY from the memory subsystem's noise, and stays compatible with UFS 4.x hardware.
claims.source: JEDEC press release, 26 February 2026
claims.conditions: Features attributed to the JEDEC and MIPI collaboration
claims.note: 'Enhanced signal integrity through integrated link equalization'; 'a distinct power supply rail to provide noise isolation between PHY and memory subsystem'; '46.6 Gb/s per lane per direction and supporting up to ~10.8 GB/s effective read/write operation for UFS 5.0 over 2 M-PHY lanes'. Read on jedec.org on 18 Oct 2026.
claims.source_title: JEDEC — UFS 5.0 announcement

claims.statement: M-PHY v5.0 (announced 14 December 2021) added HS-G5 at 23.32 Gbps per lane (93.28 Gbps over four lanes), high-speed startup, eye monitoring and new equalisation attributes, and is backward compatible through v4.1. M-PHY v6.0 (December 2025) adds HS-G6 using PAM-4 at up to 46.694 Gbps per lane, a 1b1b line encoding that cuts PHY coding overhead below 10%, and optional link equalisation and training.
claims.source: MIPI Alliance M-PHY specification page; M-PHY v5.0 press release (14 December 2021)
claims.conditions: Public summaries; the specifications are members-only
claims.note: M-PHY page: 'New high-speed gear (HS-G6), using PAM-4 signaling scheme, doubling the bandwidth of the interface to a maximum of 46.694 Gbps per lane'; 'New 1b1b line encoding for HS-G6, improving throughput efficiency by reducing PHY coding overhead to below 10%'. Press release: 'M-PHY v5.0 is backward compatible through v4.1'.
claims.source_title: MIPI Alliance — M-PHY specification page

claims.statement: In M-PHY, terminated signalling is mandatory in high-speed (HS) mode and unterminated signalling optional, with large and small amplitude settings, and 8b10b coding limits common-mode noise. An HS receiver locks its CDR on a synchronisation sequence whose length the specification leaves to the application; its low-speed PWM mode embeds the clock in the data and needs no CDR. Leaving the STALL state between HS bursts takes nanoseconds, while leaving HIBERN8, the ultra-low-power state, takes hundreds to thousands of microseconds, programmably.
claims.source: Mixel and ST-Ericsson, "M-PHY Benefits and Challenges" (A. Takla, C. Bertholom)
claims.conditions: Written for M-PHY v1.0, about 2011; later versions added HS-G4 to HS-G6 and high-speed startup, so the timings are indicative of the state structure, not limits for UFS 4.0
claims.note: 'HS operation support of terminated operation is mandatory, while support for un-terminated operation is optional'; 'A synchronization sequence locks the receiver CDR phase and frequency'; 'The M-PHY specification does not dictate this sequence length'; Hibern8: 'takes hundreds to thousands of microseconds'; HS Stall: 'a fast transition in the range of ns'. PWM: 'Since the clock is embedded in PWM data, no Clock/Data Recovery (CDR) or even a PLL is needed.' That 8b10b still applies up to HS-G5 is supported by M-PHY v6.0 introducing 1b1b specifically to cut coding overhead below 10% (C-162), and by JEDEC's ~4.2 GB/s being about 90% of two HS-G5 lanes after 8b10b.
claims.source_title: Mixel — M-PHY benefits and challenges

claims.statement: M-PHY transmitter conformance is specified at the transmitter pins, with HS-G4 and HS-G5 eyes accumulated to 1e-6 and extrapolated to a bit error ratio of 1e-12. Receiver conformance sends a calibrated stressed signal, including a conformant ISI channel, and requires zero errors over at least 3e10 bits for a 1e-10 target or 3e12 bits for 1e-12.
claims.source: Tektronix, 'MIPI M-PHY Transmitter Test Solutions' datasheet (TekExpress M-PHY Tx, MPHY50/MPHY40); Granite River Labs, 'MIPI M-PHY Receiver Conformance Testing for Physical Layer Evaluation' (24 September 2024)
claims.conditions: Test-equipment vendors describing the M-PHY v5.0 conformance test suite; the limits themselves are in the members-only CTS
claims.note: Tektronix: 'measurements are specified at the TX pins'; 'the eye diagram shows the accumulated eye at BER E-6 and extrapolated eye ... at BER of 1E-12'. GRL: 'observable bits of minimum 3E+10 (@ 1E-10 target BER) or 3E+12 (@ 1E-12 target BER)'; the device 'must report zero received errors'.
claims.source_title: Granite River Labs — MIPI M-PHY receiver conformance testing

claims.statement: JESD209-5B (July 2021) added TX/RX equalisation and Adaptive Refresh Management to LPDDR5, and introduced LPDDR5X as an optional extension aimed at higher bandwidth and a simpler architecture.
claims.source: JEDEC press release, 28 July 2021
claims.conditions: The announcement; the standard itself has not been read
claims.note: Read on jedec.org. The release names the equalisation but not where it sits or how it is set; C-167 and C-53 fill in what vendors describe. The same release quotes Samsung describing LPDDR5X as substantial bandwidth expansion "with minimal IP change"; that is a member’s description, not a compatibility guarantee, and the page presents it as such.
claims.source_title: JEDEC — JESD209-5B announcement: LPDDR5 update and LPDDR5X

claims.statement: JESD209-5 (February 2019) introduced WCK and a read strobe RDQS, a 250 mV signalling voltage, non-target ODT for DQ, DFE, selectable background or command-based ZQ calibration, and dynamic frequency and voltage scaling of core and I/O, and a programmable bank organisation: 8 banks, 4 bank groups of 4 banks, or 16 banks.
claims.source: JEDEC press release, 19 February 2019
claims.conditions: The announcement of the first LPDDR5 edition
claims.note: Read on jedec.org, from the list of key specification updates. The release also lets CK, WCK and RDQS each be differential or single-ended.
claims.source_title: JEDEC — JESD209-5 (LPDDR5) publication announcement

claims.statement: LPDDR5X adds the 7500 and 8533 MT/s bins (CK 937.5 and 1066.5 MHz, WCK 3750 and 4266.5 MHz), a unified non-target ODT behaviour required of every device for dual-rank reads, per-byte transmit pre-emphasis, receiver offset calibration training, per-pin DFE, and extended latencies, and drops the 8-bank mode.
claims.source: Cadence blog (S. Sharma), "Taking LPDDR5 to the Next Level", 19 February 2021
claims.conditions: A verification-IP vendor’s summary written while LPDDR5X was being finalised
claims.note: Read on community.cadence.com. Written before JESD209-5B was published, so later editions may differ. The DRAM-side DFE and pre-emphasis are optional per device and advertised in mode registers (C-53).
claims.source_title: Cadence — Taking LPDDR5 to the next level (LPDDR5X differences)

claims.statement: LPDDR4 and LPDDR4X run to 4267 Mbps with CK and a bidirectional DQS at the same frequency, at an I/O voltage of 1.1 V (LPDDR4) or 0.6 V (LPDDR4X); LPDDR5 DRAMs have a single-tap DFE on write data.
claims.source: Synopsys LPDDR5 technical bulletin (January 2020), table 1 and the clocking and DFE sections
claims.conditions: An IP vendor’s comparison table
claims.note: Read on synopsys.com. The table lists "1.1V / 0.6V I/O" for LPDDR4, which is the LPDDR4 and LPDDR4X pair. The same bulletin gives LPDDR5 I/O at 0.5 V and 0.3 V under voltage scaling (C-63 agrees).
claims.source_title: Synopsys — Key features designers should know about LPDDR5

claims.statement: Samsung announced an LPDDR5X DRAM running at up to 10.7 Gb/s in April 2024, on a 12 nm-class process, with mass production planned for the second half of 2024.
claims.source: Samsung Newsroom, "Samsung Develops Industry’s Fastest 10.7Gbps LPDDR5X DRAM, Optimized for AI Applications", 17 April 2024
claims.conditions: One vendor’s product; whether 10.7 Gb/s is a bin in a JEDEC edition is in JESD209-5C, which has not been read
claims.note: Read on news.samsung.com. Verifies the product announcement, not a JEDEC speed bin.
claims.source_title: Samsung — 10.7 Gb/s LPDDR5X announcement

claims.statement: One FPGA vendor’s LPDDR5 memory-down guideline routes DQ as 40 ohm stripline on upper layers, with via transitions no deeper than 50 mil and at most 3.0 inches in total, and warns that deep-layer via transitions raise crosstalk.
claims.source: Altera, External Memory Interfaces Agilex 7 M-Series FPGA IP User Guide, 8.3.7.2 Routing Guidelines for LPDDR5 Memory Down Topology, table 276
claims.conditions: One vendor, one platform, single or dual rank; a phone SoC’s guide will differ
claims.note: Read on docs.altera.com (version 26.1.1). The same section says LPDDR5 eye margin is sensitive to crosstalk, especially on deep layers, and that skew matching includes package as well as PCB routing.
claims.source_title: Altera — LPDDR5 memory-down routing guidelines (Agilex 7 M-Series EMIF)

claims.statement: JESD406-5 (August 2024) defines the SPD contents of LPDDR5/5X modules, including CAMM2s, so that firmware can read a module’s capacity, speed and I/O configuration; CAMM2 raw card E is an LPDDR5/5X module of one or two ranks organised as eight sub-channels of x16 I/O.
claims.source: JEDEC press release, "JEDEC Releases New Standard for LPDDR5/5X Serial Presence Detect (SPD) Contents", 22 August 2024
claims.conditions: The announcement; the release said the raw card E design itself was still in process
claims.note: Read on jedec.org. Eight x16 sub-channels are 128 data bits, which is the width the page uses for a CAMM2 in its bandwidth table.
claims.source_title: JEDEC — LPDDR5/5X SPD contents (JESD406-5) announcement

claims.statement: PS-007A (October 2024) is JEDEC’s LPDDR5 CAMM2 connector performance standard, free to download; JEDEC lists better signal integrity and RFI, lower power and a 50% smaller form factor at similar height as its benefits over a DDR5 SODIMM connector.
claims.source: JEDEC press release, "JEDEC Publishes LPDDR5 CAMM2 Connector Performance Standard", 31 October 2024
claims.conditions: The announcement; the standard’s electrical limits have not been read
claims.note: Read on jedec.org. The benefits are JEDEC’s own description, and the page presents them as such. The standard itself was read on 19 Oct 2026; its limits are C-179 and C-180.
claims.source_title: JEDEC — LPDDR5 CAMM2 connector performance standard (PS-007A) announcement

claims.statement: An LP5 CAMM2 (LPDDR5 or LPDDR5X) is x128, eight x16 sub-channels; a channel is four 16-bit sub-channels, each with its own clock, command, address, chip selects and data. LP5 CAMM2s are expected to start at 6400 MT/s and rise with the DRAM, and the module covers the whole connector with the DRAM placed over it.
claims.source: JEDEC JESD318B, Compression Attached Memory Module (CAMM2) Common Standard, Version 1.14, November 2025, §1 Scope, Table 1, §6.1, §6.2
claims.conditions: The standard; a given module’s rate is in its SPD and data sheet
claims.note: Read from the standard (a free download after JEDEC registration); the copy is kept private and the page paraphrases it. The standard names the LPDDR5 read strobe DQS in its signal table (corrected in v1.13 to match the DRAM definition); the page calls it RDQS, as elsewhere.
claims.source_title: JEDEC — JESD318B CAMM2 Common Standard (v1.14, Nov 2025)

claims.statement: CAMM2 connector pins sit on 1.0 x 1.38 mm centres in 14 rows; the dual-channel variations have 356 pins with ground shields between rows, or 644 or 666 pins without; an LP5 CAMM2 commonly uses a shieldless variation, and a solid 17.4 x 78.4 mm ground plane under the connector carries no traces because shield segments break at supplier-dependent places.
claims.source: JEDEC JESD318B, Compression Attached Memory Module (CAMM2) Common Standard, Version 1.14, November 2025, Table 1, §6.5, §6.15.1
claims.conditions: Connector geometry from the module standard; the connector’s electrical performance is in PS-007A, not read
claims.note: Read from the standard (a free download after JEDEC registration); the copy is kept private and the page paraphrases it. The no-traces rule is given as a module requirement and a motherboard recommendation.
claims.source_title: JEDEC — JESD318B CAMM2 Common Standard (v1.14, Nov 2025)

claims.statement: An LP5 CAMM2 carries a PMIC5200 that makes VDD2H 1.05 V, VDD2L 0.9 V, VDDQ 0.5 V and VDD1 1.8 V from a 5 V input; VDDQ may be split-rail (required: separate regulators for SoC and DRAM) or common (optional: one regulator). Split rails can drift to opposite ends of their tolerance and erode I/O margin; a common rail shares one tolerance between board and module, and in range 1 the host must hold 0.477 to 0.577 V (0.507 V typical) at the footprint, which includes 7 mV for connector and module plane drop.
claims.source: JEDEC JESD318B, Compression Attached Memory Module (CAMM2) Common Standard, Version 1.14, November 2025, §4.1, Table 9, §4.3, Table 12
claims.conditions: The module standard; DRAM limits are in JESD209-5
claims.note: Read from the standard (a free download after JEDEC registration); the copy is kept private and the page paraphrases it. The first LP5 CAMM2 designs use a discrete VDDQ regulator, and then support neither VDD2L nor a 0.3 V VDDQ. Range 2 (0.3 V class) is for ODT disabled.
claims.source_title: JEDEC — JESD318B CAMM2 Common Standard (v1.14, Nov 2025)

claims.statement: The JESD318B reference 10-layer CAMM2 stackup has LP5 data, command and chip select at 40 ohm +/-5 single-ended, and every signal group references ground; its simulation example uses a 40 mm motherboard at 40 ohm (75 ohm differential for clocks and strobes) and a 34 ohm driver; CAMM2s have no DQ or CA stub resistors, and the LP5 ZQ resistor is 240 ohm +/-1% to VDDQ.
claims.source: JEDEC JESD318B, Compression Attached Memory Module (CAMM2) Common Standard, Version 1.14, November 2025, §6.4 Table 18, §6.10.4, §6.10.5, §6.11.1, Table 22
claims.conditions: Reference designs and a simulation example, not limits a product must meet
claims.note: Read from the standard (a free download after JEDEC registration); the copy is kept private and the page paraphrases it. The standard says reference stackups only demonstrate feasibility; vendors define their own. Its total thickness is not quoted on the page: the reference stackup table sums to 1.40 mm, while PS-007A specifies a connector mated to a 1.20 mm nominal module.
claims.source_title: JEDEC — JESD318B CAMM2 Common Standard (v1.14, Nov 2025)

claims.statement: CAMM2 length matching offsets each connector row by 1 mm so that the motherboard-plus-module path is matched rather than each board separately; on the LP5 module, DQ to WCK per x16 is held to -2 to +3.2 mm, DQ to the read strobe per x8 to +/-0.6 mm, WCK to CK to -1 to +2 mm, DQ within a byte to under 0.025 mm and each differential pair to under 0.05 mm; full-channel rules come from the SoC supplier.
claims.source: JEDEC JESD318B, Compression Attached Memory Module (CAMM2) Common Standard, Version 1.14, November 2025, §6.5, §6.6, Table 21
claims.conditions: Module-side bounds, stated as a task-group starting point
claims.note: Read from the standard (a free download after JEDEC registration); the copy is kept private and the page paraphrases it. The page converts the bounds to time at 6.7 ps/mm, which is its own assumption, not the standard’s.
claims.source_title: JEDEC — JESD318B CAMM2 Common Standard (v1.14, Nov 2025)

claims.statement: JESD318B asks that signal vias not sit close together (differential pairs excepted), with power or ground vias between them, that vias of different channels be at least 2 mm apart to limit channel-to-channel crosstalk, and that ground vias sit close to signal vias for the return current.
claims.source: JEDEC JESD318B, Compression Attached Memory Module (CAMM2) Common Standard, Version 1.14, November 2025, §6.10.1, §6.15.3
claims.conditions: Module layout requirements and recommendations
claims.note: Read from the standard (a free download after JEDEC registration); the copy is kept private and the page paraphrases it.
claims.source_title: JEDEC — JESD318B CAMM2 Common Standard (v1.14, Nov 2025)

claims.statement: PS-007A defines a compression-mount LPDDR5 CAMM2 connector on a 1.38 x 1.0 mm pitch for channels beyond 6.4 GT/s, mated to a 1.20 mm nominal module; each contact has at most 50 mohm initial resistance and carries 1.0 A at a 30 C rise.
claims.source: JEDEC PS-007A, LPDDR5 CAMM2 Connector Performance Standard, Issue A, July 2024, §1 Scope, §1.1, Table 6
claims.conditions: Connector requirements; the module and system are separate standards
claims.note: Read from the standard (a free download after JEDEC registration); the copy is kept private and the page paraphrases it. Contact resistance may rise by no more than 20 mohm after stress.
claims.source_title: JEDEC — PS-007A LPDDR5 CAMM2 Connector Performance Standard (Jul 2024)

claims.statement: PS-007A limits the connector, measured with its pads and 0.25 mm micro-vias at a 40 ohm reference, to insertion loss better than -0.40 dB from 3 to 8 GHz, return loss below -20 dB from 2 to 6 GHz, NEXT below -34 dB from 4 to 6 GHz, FEXT below -38 dB from 3 to 5 GHz and -36 dB from 5 to 7 GHz, and power-sum FEXT below -35 dB from 3 to 5 GHz and -32 dB from 5 to 7 GHz, all specified to 20 GHz; in the time domain its impedance must stay within 40 to 45 ohm for a 40 ps (10-90%) edge.
claims.source: JEDEC PS-007A, LPDDR5 CAMM2 Connector Performance Standard, Issue A, July 2024, §10.1 Table 7, §10.2 Table 8, Annex D
claims.conditions: The connector with its launch, not a full channel; the page quotes only the bands that hold LPDDR5X’s Nyquist frequencies
claims.note: Read from the standard (a free download after JEDEC registration); the copy is kept private and the page paraphrases it. The page converts the dB limits to fractions of a 250 mV swing (C-166) as a sense of scale; that conversion is the page’s, not the standard’s.
claims.source_title: JEDEC — PS-007A LPDDR5 CAMM2 Connector Performance Standard (Jul 2024)

claims.statement: One FPGA vendor's DDR5 memory-down guideline routes DQ and DQS as 45 ohm stripline on upper layers, at most 4.5 inches in total to the DRAM for single or dual rank; clock and command/address run 40 ohm from the FPGA, at most 4.0 inches to the first DRAM and 6.6 inches to the last, with the fly-by segments between DRAMs at 50 ohm or more.
claims.source: Altera, External Memory Interfaces Agilex 7 M-Series FPGA IP User Guide (version 26.1.1), 7.4.8.2 Routing Guidelines for DDR5 Memory Down, tables 247 and 249
claims.source_title: Altera — DDR5 memory-down routing guidelines (Agilex 7 M-Series EMIF)
claims.conditions: One vendor, one platform, its default stackup; a CPU or SoC vendor's guide will differ
claims.note: Read on docs.altera.com. Table 247 is published as an image and was read from it: target Zse 40 ohm on the main CLK and CMD/ADDR/CTRL segment, 50+ on the between-DRAM segment, 45 on DQ and DQS. Table 249 says data must be on upper layers to avoid long-via vertical crosstalk, for 65 or 120 mil boards, and that the FPGA package length is under 34 mm. The guide's lengths assume Altera's default stackup.

claims.statement: The same guideline, for one DDR5 UDIMM, RDIMM or SODIMM per channel, routes DQ as 50 ohm stripline at most 4.5 inches in total and clock and command/address at 40 ohm, and asks for DQ matched to its DQS within +/-3.5 ps, package routing included.
claims.source: Altera, External Memory Interfaces Agilex 7 M-Series FPGA IP User Guide (version 26.1.1), 7.4.8.3 Routing Guidelines for DDR5 RDIMM, UDIMM, and SODIMM Configurations, tables 250 to 252
claims.source_title: Altera — DDR5 RDIMM, UDIMM and SODIMM routing guidelines (Agilex 7 M-Series EMIF)
claims.conditions: One DIMM per channel, two ranks per DIMM, one vendor's default stackup
claims.note: Read on docs.altera.com; tables 250 and 251 are images. Table 251 states its limits in time at an assumed 170 ps/in and requires package length to be included; its right-hand column is cut off in the published image, so only the DQ-to-DQS row is used. The guide gives no two-DIMM-per-channel table.

claims.statement: JEDEC's DDR5 MRDIMM multiplexes ranks to raise bandwidth with no extra physical connections, is planned to deliver up to twice the peak bandwidth of native DRAM, keeps RDIMM's capacity and RAS features, and uses standard DDR5 DRAM, form factor and pinout, SPD and PMIC, with platform compatibility with RDIMM.
claims.source: JEDEC press release, "JEDEC Unveils Plans for DDR5 MRDIMM and LPDDR6 CAMM Standards to Propel High-Performance Computing and AI", 22 July 2024
claims.source_title: JEDEC — DDR5 MRDIMM plans announcement (July 2024)
claims.conditions: A plan at the time; JEDEC notes standards may change
claims.note: Read on jedec.org. The release also announces a Tall MRDIMM form factor with twice the single-die packages.

claims.statement: In April 2026 JEDEC published JESD82-552, a DDR5 multiplexed-rank data buffer (MDB), said the matching registering clock driver (JESD82-542, MRCD) was expected soon, and said Gen2 DDR5 MRDIMM raw cards targeting 12,800 MT/s were in development.
claims.source: JEDEC press release, "JEDEC Advances DDR5 MRDIMM Ecosystem with New Memory Interface Logic and Expanded MRDIMM Roadmap", 30 April 2026
claims.source_title: JEDEC — DDR5 MRDIMM roadmap announcement (April 2026)
claims.conditions: 12,800 MT/s is a target for designs in development, not a published bin
claims.note: Read on jedec.org. The release also says the MRDIMM Gen2 module standard is nearing completion and Gen3 is being looked at.

claims.statement: Rambus describes an MRDIMM as multiplexing two ranks of DRAM so the host bus runs at twice the data rate of the DRAM devices, with an MRCD that addresses the two ranks on alternate clock cycles and ten data buffers (MDBs) steering the data; in the same announcement it introduced an RCD for RDIMMs at 8000 MT/s.
claims.source: Rambus press release, "Rambus Unveils Industry-First Complete Chipsets for Next-Generation DDR5 MRDIMMs and RDIMMs", 15 October 2024
claims.source_title: Rambus — DDR5 MRDIMM 12800 and RDIMM 8000 chipsets announcement
claims.conditions: One interface-chip vendor's products and description
claims.note: Read on rambus.com. The release says the MRDIMM uses the same physical connections as a DDR5 RDIMM and names MRDIMM 12800 and RDIMM 8000 chipsets.

claims.statement: Lenovo Press: by running two ranks at once an MRDIMM delivers 128 bytes per access against a regular DDR5 DIMM's 64; JEDEC expects Gen1 MRDIMMs at 8800 MT/s, Gen2 at 12,800 and Gen3 at 17,600; Xeon 6 servers with P-cores support them.
claims.source: Lenovo Press LP2028, "Introduction to MRDIMM Memory Technology", A. Rossouw, updated 25 February 2025
claims.source_title: Lenovo Press — Introduction to MRDIMM memory technology
claims.conditions: A system vendor's summary of JEDEC's roadmap
claims.note: Read on lenovopress.lenovo.com. Only the generation rates and the 128-byte access are used; the paper rounds bandwidths loosely (36 GB/s at 4800), so the page computes its own.

claims.statement: DDR5 DRAMs store 8 ECC bits for every 128 data bits and correct single-bit errors in their own array; this on-die ECC gives no protection against errors on the DDR channel, so it is paired with side-band ECC for end-to-end protection.
claims.source: Synopsys article, "Error Correction Code (ECC) in DDR Memories", V. Sankaranarayanan, 19 October 2020
claims.source_title: Synopsys — Error correction code (ECC) in DDR memories
claims.conditions: DDR5 on-die ECC as described by an IP vendor
claims.note: Read on synopsys.com. Agrees with the 128 + 8 on-die ECC in C-45. The article does not say how on-die corrections are reported, so the page says nothing about that.

claims.statement: JESD318B DDR5 CAMM2s: a single-channel module carries 64 data bits as two 32-bit subchannels (72 with ECC) and can be stacked; a dual-channel module carries 128 bits as four subchannels and cannot. On the module, CK, command/address and CS run fly-by, matched from the connector to each DRAM; the lead-in section is routed at a lower impedance than the loaded section to reduce the discontinuity at the first load; microstrip lengths are divided by 1.1 to give a stripline-equivalent length; and on two-rank modules the CK and CS segments between DRAMs are lengthened because command/address has two loads per node. DQ is matched to its DQS within +/-0.025 mm, and a clock driver sits on the module.
claims.source: JEDEC JESD318B, Compression Attached Memory Module (CAMM2) Common Standard, Version 1.14, November 2025, §2, §6.1, §6.2, §6.6 Table 20, §6.7.1 to §6.7.4
claims.source_title: JEDEC — JESD318B CAMM2 Common Standard (v1.14, Nov 2025)
claims.conditions: CAMM2 modules; the module-side rules, not the motherboard's
claims.note: Read from the standard (a free download after JEDEC registration); the copy is kept private and the page paraphrases it. The lead-in rule may not be needed for short lead-ins (the standard gives under 25 mm as an example) and is to be decided by simulation. Table 20's CS-to-CK row is not quoted: its bound reads +/-0.0025 mm, which looks like a typographical slip.

claims.statement: In April 2026 JEDEC previewed features planned for the next version of JESD209-6: x12 and an additional x6 sub-channel mode, allowing more die per package and higher capacity per component and per channel; a flexible metadata carve-out; densities beyond the LPDDR5/5X maximum; and, in development, an LPDDR6 SOCAMM2 module standard succeeding today's LPDDR5X SOCAMM2 and an LPDDR6 processing-in-memory (PIM) standard.
claims.source: JEDEC press release, "JEDEC Previews LPDDR6 Roadmap Expanding LPDDR into Data Centers and Processing-in-Memory", 22 April 2026
claims.source_title: JEDEC — LPDDR6 roadmap preview (April 2026)
claims.conditions: Planned features for an unpublished revision; JEDEC notes standards may change
claims.note: Read on jedec.org. The release does not give data rates for the new modes or the modules.

claims.statement: In July 2024 JEDEC said its JC-45 committee was developing a next-generation CAMM for LPDDR6, a follow-on to JESD318 CAMM2, targeting a maximum speed greater than 14.4 GT/s, with a 24-bit subchannel, a 48-bit channel and a connector array.
claims.source: JEDEC press release, "JEDEC Unveils Plans for DDR5 MRDIMM and LPDDR6 CAMM Standards to Propel High-Performance Computing and AI", 22 July 2024
claims.source_title: JEDEC — DDR5 MRDIMM and LPDDR6 CAMM plans announcement (July 2024)
claims.conditions: A plan at the time of the release
claims.note: Read on jedec.org (also the source of C-183 on the DDR5 page).

claims.statement: Samsung's LPDDR6, a CES 2026 Innovation Award honoree, runs at up to 10.7 Gb/s with capacities up to 16 GB and about 21% better energy efficiency than the previous generation; Samsung says it is developing an LPDDR6-based SOCAMM module and LPDDR6-PIM.
claims.source: Samsung Semiconductor Newsroom, "[CES Innovation Awards 2026 Honoree] LPDDR6: World's First Next-Gen LPDDR Optimized for High-Performing On-Device AI", 8 January 2026
claims.source_title: Samsung Semiconductor — LPDDR6 CES 2026 Innovation Award interview
claims.conditions: A vendor's own product claims, from internal test results
claims.note: Read on news.samsungsemiconductor.com. The efficiency figure is attributed to split supplies, DVFS, dynamic efficiency mode and a PMIC; the page quotes only the rate and that the efficiency is claimed. Trade-press reports of validation on a specific phone SoC are not used.

claims.statement: Samsung's JEDEC workshop slides chart LPDDR data bandwidth for a 64-bit LPDDR5X interface at 8.5, 9.6 and 10.7 Gb/s (68.3, 76.8 and 85.6 GB/s) against a 96-bit LPDDR6 interface at 10.7, 12.8 and 14.4 Gb/s (114.1, 136.5 and 153.6 GB/s).
claims.source: Samsung (Seunghyun Moon), "LPDDR6 Key Architecture", JEDEC LPDDR6 Workshop, 8 April 2025, slide "High Bandwidth requirement on LPDDR"
claims.source_title: Samsung — LPDDR6 Key Architecture (JEDEC LPDDR6 Workshop, April 2025)
claims.conditions: A vendor chart; widths and rates as plotted
claims.note: Read from the slide text. The LPDDR6 figures equal rate x 96 / 8 x 256/288, i.e. data bits only, which is how the page computes its table; the 12.8 Gb/s point is used as a label, not as a JEDEC bin.

claims.statement: UCIe's key-metric targets for ESD are 30 V CDM on a standard package and 5 V CDM on an advanced package, heading below 3 V; UCIe-3D starts at 5 V CDM, and wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding may need no ESD protection at all.
claims.source: UCIe Consortium overview deck (2025), Key Metrics with UCIe 3.0
claims.source_title: UCIe Consortium — overview deck, 2025, with the key metrics for UCIe 3.0
claims.conditions: Targets in a consortium overview, not specification limits
claims.note: Read from the key-metrics slide text, which also lists reliability as 0 < FIT << 1 for both planar options.

claims.statement: UCIe's physical layer includes lane repair and lane reversal; because microbumps cannot be probed, die and package test use other bumps such as JTAG or a UCIe-S link, repair is supported at assembly and in the field, and UCIe 2.0 adds a test, debug and management infrastructure for use in the lab and field without an analyser or oscilloscope. UCIe-3D uses cluster-level repair. A UCIe-S x16 sideband carries 800 Mb/s per direction.
claims.source: UCIe Consortium overview deck (2025), "Scope of UCIe Specification", "UCIe 2.0: Testability, Manageability, Debug" and "UCIe 2.0: Vertical Chiplets with UCIe-3D"
claims.source_title: UCIe Consortium — overview deck, 2025, with the key metrics for UCIe 3.0
claims.conditions: As described in a consortium overview; the specification itself has not been read
claims.note: Read from the slide text.

claims.statement: UCIe's key-metric targets give low-power entry and exit of 0.5 ns below 16 GT/s and 0.5 to 1 ns above 24 GT/s on the planar options, and 0 ns for UCIe-3D, which has no preamble or post-amble; areal bandwidth density is 22-192 GB/s/mm2 for UCIe-S and 188-1646 for UCIe-A at 110 and 45 um pitches.
claims.source: UCIe Consortium overview deck (2025), Key Metrics with UCIe 3.0
claims.source_title: UCIe Consortium — overview deck, 2025, with the key metrics for UCIe 3.0
claims.conditions: Targets in a consortium overview
claims.note: Read from the key-metrics slide text.
